overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Calendar Behind the Mishna
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 9a–9b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵין שְׁנַת לְבָנָה פְּחוּתָה מִשְּׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת וַחֲמִשִּׁים וּשְׁתַּיִם יוֹם, וְלֹא יְתֵירָה עַל שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת וַחֲמִשִּׁים וְשִׁשָּׁה יוֹם
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues the calendrical sugya opened by yesterday's mishna, that a year has no fewer than four full (thirty-day) months and no more than eight. Rav Huna and Ulla disagree about which figure — full or deficient months — the mishna's 'no more than eight' actually caps, each explaining why nine would embarrass the court by making the new moon of Tishrei visibly out of step with Rosh HaShana. A baraita citing Aḥerim's fixed four- (or five-, in a leap year) weekday gap between one year's festivals and the next is examined, together with Rava's point that it shows the calendar need not wait strictly on eyewitness testimony. Shmuel then fixes the range of a lunar year at 352 to 356 days, a claim tested against how a Nazirite vow 'for the days of a lunar year' is counted, and the daf closes with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's own puzzling case of nine deficient months whose new moon nonetheless appeared exactly on time.

slides.title: 🌕 Rav Huna vs. Ulla — Full Months or Deficient Months?
slides.subtitle: Two readings of the mishna's cap: 'not more than eight'

lines.speaker: Rav Huna
lines.text: The mishna's cap of eight applies to FULL, thirty-day months — no more than eight can be established in a single year.

lines.speaker: Ulla
lines.text: No — the cap of eight applies instead to DEFICIENT, twenty-nine-day months. The mishna's earlier floor of four full months is explained by THIS reason.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: To each: why not allow a ninth such month?

lines.speaker: Both answer
lines.text: Either way, a ninth would push the new moon of Tishrei three days out of alignment with Rosh HaShana — inviting the public to accuse the court of fixing the calendar arbitrarily.

callout.label: Underlying source:
callout.text: The dispute traces to a baraita on how many days the intercalated (leap) month adds: the first tanna says thirty; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says twenty-nine. Rav Huna follows the latter, Ulla the former.

slides.title: 🔭 Even Eight Should Show a Gap — So Why No Complaints?
slides.subtitle: Rav Mesharshiyya's resolution keeps the discrepancy invisible

nodes.content: ❓ Even eight full months should push the new moon two days off from Rosh HaShana — wouldn't people notice and deride the court?
💡 Rav Mesharshiyya: if the PRIOR year was already a leap year, its extra month offsets one of this year's extra full months — leaving only a one-day gap

columns.label: For full months
columns.content: A gap of just one day goes unnoticed by the public

columns.label: For deficient months
columns.content: People simply assume witnesses saw the new moon a day earlier and it was overlooked

slides.title: 📅 The Baraita of Aḥerim — a Fixed Weekday Gap
slides.subtitle: How far does Rosh HaShana or Shavuot shift on the weekly calendar from one year to the next?

callout.label: Why it matters (Rava):
callout.text: This fixed, calculable gap teaches that the calendar need not wait strictly on eyewitness testimony of the new moon — a predictable calculation can stand in its place.

slides.title: 🔢 Shmuel's Range for a Lunar Year — and the Nazirite Challenge
slides.subtitle: 352 to 356 days, tested against a real halakhic case

steps.content: 1️⃣ Shmuel: a lunar year is never fewer than 352 days, nor more than 356
2️⃣ How: both 'variable' months full → 356 days; both deficient → 352 days; the ordinary alternation of full and deficient → 354 days
3️⃣ Challenge: a baraita says a Nazirite who vows 'for the days of a lunar year' always counts exactly 354 days — so why not sometimes 356, per Shmuel's own range?
4️⃣ Resolution: vow language follows common, everyday usage, and most lunar years run 354 days — that is the default meaning of the phrase, whatever the technical range

slides.title: 🤔 Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's Puzzling Year
slides.subtitle: A real incident that seems to defy the whole system
slides.label: The incident:
slides.text: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once established nine consecutive deficient (twenty-nine-day) months in a single year — a count that, by the Gemara's own logic, should have pushed the new moon three days out of alignment with Rosh HaShana. Yet the new moon was sighted exactly on time. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi expressed his own astonishment at this. His son, Rabbi Shimon, offered the resolution: perhaps the preceding year had itself been a leap year, whose extra month absorbed the discrepancy — the same principle Rav Mesharshiyya used earlier to explain why an apparent gap does not always surface.

summary.principle: The mishna's simple floor and ceiling on intercalated months rests on a precise lunar calculation: the court must keep the new moon's actual appearance from visibly drifting away from the calendar's fixed dates, and every apparent exception — a stretch of eight full or eight deficient months, or even Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's nine — is shown to be absorbed by the accounting of the surrounding years.

flowSteps.content: 🌕 Rav Huna: cap of eight applies to full months; Ulla: cap of eight applies to deficient months — both to prevent a 3-day drift
🔭 Even a smaller apparent gap is absorbed by the prior year's leap-month accounting, or goes unnoticed by the public

columns.content: 📅 Aḥerim: festivals shift a fixed 4 (or 5, in a leap year) weekdays each year — the calendar can override eyewitness sighting
🔢 Shmuel: a lunar year runs 352–356 days; Nazirite vow language defaults to the common 354

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: the fixed floor and ceiling on intercalated months exists to keep the rabbinic calendar credibly aligned with the observable new moon

quiz.q: What is the core disagreement between Rav Huna and Ulla about the mishna's phrase 'not more than eight'?
o: Rav Huna holds it caps the number of FULL (thirty-day) months at eight; Ulla holds it caps the number of DEFICIENT (twenty-nine-day) months at eight
They disagree about whether the number is seven or eight
Rav Huna says the cap applies only to leap years; Ulla says it applies to every year
They disagree about how many months are in a year altogether
quiz.e: Rav Huna reads the mishna's ceiling as limiting full, thirty-day months to eight per year, while Ulla reads it as limiting deficient, twenty-nine-day months to eight.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara say the Sages avoided establishing nine full (or nine deficient) months in a single year?
o: Because nine months is astronomically impossible
Because it would push the new moon of Tishrei three days out of alignment with Rosh HaShana, inviting the public to accuse the court of fixing dates arbitrarily
Because nine months would make the year too short for all the festivals
Because the Torah explicitly forbids more than eight such months
quiz.e: The Gemara's concern throughout is the court's credibility: a three-day gap between the calculated new moon and its actual appearance would be conspicuous and invite derision.

quiz.q: According to the baraita of Aḥerim, what is the fixed weekday gap between one year's festivals (such as Shavuot or Rosh HaShana) and the next?
o: Four weekdays in an ordinary year, five in a leap year
Always exactly seven weekdays
Two weekdays regardless of the year type
There is no fixed gap at all
quiz.e: Aḥerim teach that an ordinary 354-day year is exactly 50 weeks and 4 days, and a leap year of 383 days is 54 weeks and 5 days, producing those fixed weekday shifts.

quiz.q: According to Shmuel, what is the range of days in a lunar year?
o: Always exactly 354 days, with no variation
No fewer than 352 days, no more than 356 days
No fewer than 350 days, no more than 360 days
Between 300 and 400 days
quiz.e: Shmuel states the lunar year ranges from 352 days (both variable months deficient) to 356 days (both variable months full), with 354 as the ordinary case.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara resolve the challenge that a Nazirite who vows 'for the days of a lunar year' always counts exactly 354 days, despite Shmuel's range reaching up to 356?
o: It rejects Shmuel's ruling entirely
Vow language follows common, everyday usage, and since most lunar years run 354 days, that figure is the vow's default meaning
356 days is used only for leap years
The Nazirite must ask a court to determine the exact count each time
quiz.e: The Gemara answers that halakhic vows are interpreted according to how ordinary people use the term, and the common lunar year is 354 days, regardless of the technical possible range.
